title: Commitment Hedge and Ephemeral Burst Contract (Dedicated Capacity) - PRD
creator: Ava Martinez
description:
Executive summary: This PRD proposes a new contract primitive for Dedicated capacity: the Commitment Hedge with Ephemeral Burst (CHEB). CHEB lets customers combine a baseline reserved commit with a transparent, short-duration burst mechanism underpinned by an escrowed credit ledger and post-burst reconciliation. The feature aims to provide predictable unit economics, safety for isolation-sensitive tenants, and a controlled runway for legitimate short spikes without expanding long-term reserved commitments.

Problem statement: Many customers want predictable latency and cost on Dedicated GPU pools, but also need to absorb short, real-world traffic spikes (marketing events, nightly batches, or ad-hoc eval runs) without overprovisioning long-lived reserved capacity. Current Dedicated semantics (hard reserves + opportunistic bursting) either force customers to buy too much capacity or rely on opaque fallback behavior that causes customer confusion and SLO surprises. Customers also want clear billing, compensatory protections for tenants adversely affected by bursts (no silent SLA degradations), and operational knobs for admins to audit and control burst behavior.

Goals: 
- Provide a contract-level primitive (CHEB) that mixes a committed baseline with an escrowed burst allowance usable for short windows (minutes to a few hours).
- Ensure transparent billing and post-burst reconciliation so customers understand cost impact and credits.
- Protect isolation guarantees for high-priority tenants via tenant-cooling windows and compensatory credits when a burst causes measurable SLI regressions.
- Expose API + Console surfaces for programmatic lease/borrow flows and operator controls.

Non-goals / out of scope: 
- Replacing primary reserved commit contracts or billing models entirely. 
- Full multi-cloud rescheduling or VM-level autoscaling (infra-level autoscale improvements are separate).
- Deep ML model-level inference optimizations (this PRD focuses on allocation, policy, and economics).

Success metrics: 
- Percentage of Dedicated customers who avoid increasing baseline reserve after using CHEB for at least three months: target >= 40%.
- Percentage reduction in overcommit churn (customers upgrading reserved tiers due to transient spikes): target 20% within 6 months.
- Mean time to reconcile (post-burst ledger settle) under 10 minutes for 95% of events.
- No customer-visible SLO regressions for P0 customers attributable to CHEB on launch (SLO regressions attributable to misconfiguration are acceptable).

Stakeholders: 
- PM: Ava Martinez (owner), 
- Eng (Serving/runtime + Orchestration): Rohit Kapoor (lead), 
- Console/UX: Maya Chen, 
- Billing/Revenue: Daniel Osei, 
- Support/Success: Priya Iyer, 
- Legal/Billing ops: Hannah Schultz.

Design principles and trade-offs: 
- Deterministic economics: CHEB must not create opaque burst charges. Using an escrow ledger (customer-funded burst credits or on-demand conversion at a transparent rate) trades short-term friction for predictability.
- Isolation-first default: High-tier customers (SLA tier A) get stronger implicit protections; default tenant-cooling windows are configurable per-contract but conservative at launch. This choice reduces risk to critical customers at cost of slightly reduced burstability.
- Simplicity of API: Expose 2 primary API calls (ReserveLease, BorrowBurst) plus a reconciliation webhook. Avoid complex per-request policy expressions at initial launch.

Requirements:
requirements: R1: Contract primitive CHEB must allow baseline commit (vGPU hours) + burst escrow (credit amount or burst-hours) to be attached to a Dedicated reservation.
R2: BorrowBurst API must atomically request ephemeral capacity for a named contract; response must include estimated cost, pre-authorized debit, and expected reconciliation timeline.
R3: Escrow ledger must be queriable via API and console with transaction-level detail and human-friendly reconciliation summaries.

R4: Tenant-cooling windows: when a burst occurs that impacts other tenants’ P0 SLOs, the system must enforce a configurable cooldown period for borrower tenant’s subsequent burst attempts and credit back compensatory credits to harmed tenants as defined by policy.
R5: Post-burst reconciliation must settle charges and credit transfers within 10 minutes for 95% of events and always within 24 hours.
R6: Console must provide a CHEB contract view, real-time escrow balance, and a timeline of burst events with per-request latency/cost deltas.
R7: Billing integration: final reconciled charges must appear in the customer invoice with a transparent line-item indicating burst consumption and compensatory credit adjustments.
R8: Admin/operator controls: operators must be able to throttle borrowing globally and per-pool, view active borrowings, and trigger manual reconciliations or rollbacks.
R9: Safety: Default contract settings must include conservative burst caps and cooldown windows; customers may opt-in to more permissive settings after an explicit intent flow.
R10: Observability: Emit events for borrow request, borrow grant, fallback invocation, reconciliation complete, and compensatory credit transfer to internal telemetry and alerting systems.
out_of_scope: O1: Dynamic kernel selection or model-level quantization guidance; those remain separate runtime efforts.
O2: Long-term market-driven pricing model changes; CHEB uses existing per-token / per-embedding cost primitives for charge calculation.
O3: Automatic vertical scaling of physical GPU clusters; infrastructure autoscale handled by infra queue.
user_stories: As an SRE for a SaaS customer, I want a way to handle surge traffic for an hourly marketing campaign without increasing my monthly commit, so I can avoid long-term cost increases.
As a Platform Admin at Redwood, I want operator controls to mute runaway burst consumers quickly, so I can protect tenant isolation and SLOs.
As a Billing owner, I want ledger-level visibility into burst usage and compensatory credits so invoices reconcile directly with events and support tickets.
As an App engineer, I want a simple API to request ephemeral capacity with an estimated cost so I can implement graceful fallbacks in my application.
api_endpoints: POST /v1/dedicated/leases - create ReserveLease (baseline + optional escrow parameters).
GET /v1/dedicated/leases/:lease_id/escrow - return ledger balance and pending transactions.
POST /v1/dedicated/leases/:lease_id/reconcile - trigger reconciliation (internal use or webhook target).
console_changes: New CHEB contract page under Dedicated -> Contracts showing baseline reservation, escrow balance, active borrows, and historical reconciliations.
Inline ‘Borrow now’ CTA with pre-checks and estimated cost modal for contract admins.
Operator dashboard with active borrow heatmap, per-pool borrow rate, and one-click mute/throttle buttons.
metrics: Primary: churn_change_reserved_commit (fraction of customers who increase baseline after CHEB use).
Safety: operator_mute_actions_per_week (monitor for tuning default limits)
rollout_plan: Phase 0 (internal alpha): small subset of internal teams + selected Enterprise customers, 2 weeks of synthetic spike exercises.
Phase 1 (beta): invite-only customers with support coverage and manual operator oversight for the first 6 weeks.
Phase 2 (general availability): publicly available with self-serve opt-in; provide migration guide for existing reserved customers.
Rollback plan: immediately revoke BorrowBurst grants and pause CHEB acceptance; reconciliations still processed for already-used credits.
Support playbook: runbook for investigating tenant impact, compensatory credit calculations, and customer communication templates.
acceptance_criteria: AC1: Create ReserveLease and BorrowBurst calls successfully provision ephemeral capacity in the Dedicated pool and return deterministic cost estimates in 95% of requests.
AC2: Escrow ledger exposes transaction history in the Console and via API; reconciled charges appear on a test invoice line-item within the billing pipeline.

AC3: Compensatory credit transfers are performed automatically when a borrow event is correlated with a downstream P0 SLO regression (heuristic to be defined in implementation), and evidence of transfer is visible in ledger and invoice test data.
AC4: Operator controls (mute/throttle) can be exercised from Console and take effect within 30 seconds for active BorrowBurst sessions.
AC5: Load test: CHEB borrow workflow survives 10,000 concurrent borrow attempts across pools without causing controller panic or >5% increase in median P50 latency for unaffected tenants.
AC6: Documentation: PRD, API spec, Console UX spec, and support runbook published and reviewed.
notes: Tradeoff: escrowed credits create a small UX friction on purchase but solve the core problem of predictable economics.
Operational concern: need throttles that operate at the scheduler level to avoid noisy-neighbor amplification; partner with ENG scheduling team for rate-limits.
Decision log: default cooldown windows set to 30 minutes for tier B, 10 minutes for tier A, and 60 minutes for tier C in alpha to protect critical tenants.
